title: Python for Scientific Development
text:
Snakemake

Problem 1: Advisor wants you to regenerate a figure from 6 months ago—what was the script? What were the parameters?
Problem 2: You changed src/core/utils.py and now you need to know which of your 500 simulation results are now invalid.
The Solution: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs).
Automation: One command (snakemake) to run everything in the correct order.
Reproducibility: The Snakefile is the documentation.

title: Python for Scientific Development
text:
Snakemake: Workflow Orchestration


The Problems

Amnesia: “I changed code; what results are now invalid?”
Lost parameters: “How did I generate this figure 6 months ago?”
Batch Hell: VACC repo littered with 10M Slurm batch files.


The Solutions

DAG Generation: Snakemake knows exactly what needs to run.
Self-Documentation: The Snakefile is the record.
Registry: High-level rules replace manual Slurm scripts.
Example: Snakefile

title: Python for Scientific Development
text:
Defensive Coding: Testing

Unit Testing: Whenever you write a significant function, define what “correct” looks like.

Shape Checks: Is the matrix the size I expect?
Analytical Baseline: Does my numerical model match a known analytical solution?
Regression: Does my “Optimized” algorithm give the same answer as my “Naive/Slow” one?

Integration Testing: Ensuring the “plumbing” works end-to-end.

The 1-Epoch Test: Does the pipeline run on a tiny dataset without crashing?
The Smoke Test: If I run for one epoch, does the loss decrease even a tiny bit?

title: Supplementary Materials
text:
The folgenden pseudocode describes the bottleneck adapter initialization used in our BERT model:
import torch.nn as nn

class Adapter(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, adapter_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.down_project = nn.Linear(input_dim, adapter_dim)
        self.act = nn.GELU()
        self.up_project = nn.Linear(adapter_dim, input_dim)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        # Bottleneck architecture
        residual = x
        x = self.down_project(x)
        x = self.act(x)
        x = self.up_project(x)
        return x + residual

The folgenden pseudocode describes the bottleneck adapter initialization used in our BERT model:
import torch.nn as nn

class Adapter(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, adapter_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.down_project = nn.Linear(input_dim, adapter_dim)
        self.act = nn.GELU()
        self.up_project = nn.Linear(adapter_dim, input_dim)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        # Bottleneck architecture
        residual = x
        x = self.down_project(x)
        x = self.act(x)
        x = self.up_project(x)
        return x + residual

title: Efficient Fine-Tuning with BERT Adapters: A Network Science Perspective
text:
Introduction
Large-scale language models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language processing (NLP). However, as mentioned in Devlin et al. (2018), full parameter fine-tuning requires significant computational resources, especially when dealing with domain-specific datasets in fields like Network Science.


Methodology
We utilize the bottleneck architecture described in Houlsby et al. (2019). This approach inserts two modules per transformer layer: one after the multi-head attention and one after the feed-forward layer. Each module consists of a down-projection, a non-linear activation, and an up-projection, effectively reducing the number of trainable parameters while maintaining representation quality.


Results and Discussion
Our experiments on the CSDS research dataset indicate that BERT adapters converge faster than full fine-tuning. We find that the structural properties of the attention weights in adapted models exhibit higher modularity compared to their fully fine-tuned counterparts, suggesting that adapters preserve the original model’s “backbone” more effectively.


Conclusion
We have demonstrated that BERT adapters are a highly efficient tool for scientific development in NLP. By minimizing the trainable parameter count, we enable more rapid iteration and experimentation on academic-scale hardware.


References


Devlin, Jacob, Ming-Wei Chang, Kenton Lee, and Kristina Toutanova. 2018. “BERT: Pre-Training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1810.04805.


Houlsby, Neil, Andrei Giurgiu, Stanislaw Jastrzebski, Brando Morrone, Quentin Larsson, Mansi Sharma, and Dmitry Kalenichenko. 2019. “Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP.” In International Conference on Machine Learning, 2790–99. PMLR.

title: I Suck At Coding
text:
Feature Creep & Portability



Phase 1: Portability

Problem: 5 collaborators on Mac, Linux, and Windows.
“Solution”: JSON configs + nested POSIX-compliant shell scripts/Python wrappers.




Phase 2: The HPC (VACC)

Problem: Local prototyping vs. Cluster batch jobs.
“Solution”: J2 templating to auto-generate .sh scripts.

title: I Suck At Coding
text:
Architecture Overkill



Data & Concurrency

Filename char limits? Build an ORM.
SQLite locking? Move to MySQL.
MySQL behind firewall? Polymorphic IO.




Total Collapse

Agnostic formatters for every possible output.
Agnostic inputs for polymorphic data classes.
The End: 2026, no publication, the framework is now so convoluted my collaborators just start writing their own code from scratch in Jupter notebooks and force-pushing to main because they hate the code.
